title: The Insidious Abuse of Stalking
summary: Josh and Chuck examine stalking as a form of psychological abuse, covering its history from the late 1980s celebrity cases (Teresa Saldana, Rebecca Schaeffer, David Letterman's stalker) through the development of anti-stalking laws, the federal definition, the Violence Against Women Act, and the three-part stalker typology (erotomania, love obsessional, simple obsessional) plus the incompetent suitor. They discuss common stalker behaviors, the link to domestic violence, international laws, safety-planning tips for victims, the idea of treating stalkers, and a listener mail segment from Ed about bed sheet thread count.

entities.name: SPARK (Stalking Prevention Awareness and Resource Center)

segments.title: Opening banter and framing stalking as abuse
segments.summary: Hosts open with light banter, then frame stalking as psychological abuse that infects a victim's life. Chuck shares a personal story about a college ex who banged on his window, and they discuss misconceptions that victims somehow deserve it.

segments.title: History of stalking awareness and celebrity cases
segments.summary: They trace how stalking became recognized in the late 1980s after celebrity cases, including movie portrayals of stalkers, the stabbing of actress Teresa Saldana, and the murder of Rebecca Schaeffer by an obsessed fan. They also mention the pretexting tactics and a website that helped people stalk, and David Letterman's stalker.

segments.title: Legal definition and the growth of anti-stalking laws
segments.summary: The hosts explain the legal gray area before the late 1980s, the federal definition of stalking based on a course of conduct causing a reasonable person to fear, and how harassment differs from stalking. They also discuss how stalking overlaps with domestic violence and the lasting harm to victims.

segments.title: Violence Against Women Act and federal protections
segments.summary: They discuss the Violence Against Women Act and its broadened law enforcement powers, the 2018 reauthorization and its pet-related provisions, a federal stalking law under Clinton, California's first state anti-stalking law, and the LAPD Threat Management Unit.

segments.title: Common stalker behaviors
segments.summary: The hosts list typical stalker behaviors: showing up, calls and texts, non-consensual communication with odd gifts, workplace stalking, threats to family and pets, trespassing and break-ins, and cyberstalking, along with financial and psychological costs to victims.

segments.title: Types of stalkers: erotomania, love obsessional, simple obsessional
segments.summary: They describe the three categories identified by early Los Angeles research: erotomania (delusional belief of being loved by a celebrity, rarely dangerous), love obsessional (obsession with an acquaintance or coworker, possibly rage on rejection), and simple obsessional (former intimate, highest risk of violence), plus the incompetent suitor subtype.

segments.title: Risk of violence, domestic abusers, and victim advice
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the high risk of violence from former intimates and domestic abusers, the limited value and enforcement issues of restraining orders, and a grim statistic about women murdered by intimate partners who had been stalked. They advise taking warnings seriously.

segments.title: Stalking laws around the world
segments.summary: The hosts note that many countries have anti-stalking laws, mention that some countries lack them, and speculate that reported rates vary with how willing women are to report stalking.

segments.title: Safety planning and treating stalkers
segments.summary: They offer practical steps for victims: documenting incidents, changing passwords and using a safe computer, safety planning, contacting local advocacy groups such as SPARK, and avoiding giving personal information. They close with the idea that stalkers can be treated through therapy.

segments.title: Listener mail from Ed about bed sheet thread count
segments.summary: A listener named Ed writes in about the short stuff episode on bedding softness, explaining that long staple cotton is softer and more durable than short staple cotton, regardless of thread count.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank Ed, invite listeners to send email, and sign off.
